questions.question: Which type of muscle is characterized by long, multinucleated fibers with peripherally located nuclei?

options.explanation: Skeletal muscle fibers are syncytial, formed by fusion of myoblasts, resulting in multiple peripheral nuclei.
Cardiac muscle has one or two central nuclei and is branched.
Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus.
These are contractile epithelial cells, not multinucleated.
Myofibroblasts have features of fibroblasts and smooth muscle, not multinucleated.

explanation.overview: Skeletal muscle is a striated voluntary muscle composed of long, cylindrical fibers formed by the fusion of myoblasts, resulting in multiple nuclei located at the periphery of the fiber.
explanation.highYield: Skeletal muscle: multinucleated, peripheral nuclei, striated, voluntary.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Muscle biopsies are used to diagnose myopathies; peripheral nuclei are a key histological feature.

questions.question: Cardiac muscle cells are connected end‑to‑end by specialized junctions called:

options.explanation: Intercalated discs contain gap junctions for electrical coupling and desmosomes for mechanical adhesion.
Gap junctions are a component of intercalated discs, not the entire structure.
Desmosomes are part of intercalated discs, but the disc includes both gap junctions and desmosomes.
Tight junctions seal epithelial cells, not cardiac muscle.
Neuromuscular junctions are between nerve and skeletal muscle.

explanation.overview: Intercalated discs are complex junctions at the ends of cardiac muscle cells, containing fascia adherens (anchoring actin), desmosomes (mechanical strength), and gap junctions (electrical coupling).
explanation.highYield: Intercalated discs = fascia adherens + desmosomes + gap junctions.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Disruption of intercalated discs occurs in myocardial infarction and cardiomyopathies.

questions.question: Smooth muscle cells are characterized by:

options.text: Spindle‑shaped cells with a single central nucleus
options.explanation: Smooth muscle cells are fusiform, uninucleate, and lack striations.

options.text: Long cylindrical cells with multiple peripheral nuclei

options.explanation: Sarcomeres are found in striated muscle.

explanation.overview: Smooth muscle is non-striated, involuntary muscle found in the walls of hollow organs. Its cells are fusiform with a single central nucleus and contain dense bodies instead of Z-lines.
explanation.highYield: Smooth muscle: spindle-shaped, single central nucleus, non-striated, involuntary.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Smooth muscle tumors (leiomyomas) are common benign tumors, especially in the uterus.

questions.question: The contractile unit of striated muscle is the:

options.explanation: Sarcomeres are repeating units between Z‑lines, containing overlapping actin and myosin filaments.
Myofilaments are the individual actin or myosin filaments.

explanation.overview: The sarcomere is the basic contractile unit of skeletal and cardiac muscle, defined as the region between two Z-lines, containing ordered arrays of thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments.
explanation.highYield: Sarcomere = Z-line to Z-line; basic contractile unit.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Sarcomere disorganization is seen in many myopathies.

questions.question: Which band of the sarcomere contains only actin filaments?

options.explanation: The I band is the region of only thin filaments (actin), and it shortens during contraction.
The A band contains the entire length of thick filaments, including overlap.
The H zone contains only thick filaments (myosin).
The M line is a central anchoring line for thick filaments.
The Z disc anchors thin filaments and marks sarcomere boundaries.

explanation.overview: The I band (isotropic band) appears light under polarized light and contains only thin (actin) filaments. During contraction, the I band shortens as actin slides over myosin.
explanation.highYield: I band = actin only; shortens during contraction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Changes in sarcomeric banding pattern can indicate muscle damage.

questions.question: The A band of the sarcomere is defined by the presence of:

options.explanation: The A band is the entire length of the thick filaments, including regions of overlap with thin filaments.
Terminal cisternae are part of the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

explanation.overview: The A band (anisotropic band) is the dark band in striated muscle, representing the full length of the thick (myosin) filaments. It remains constant in length during contraction.
explanation.highYield: A band = length of thick filaments; constant during contraction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: A band visibility is used to assess sarcomere integrity.

questions.question: During muscle contraction, which of the following occurs?

options.text: I band shortens, A band remains constant
options.explanation: The I band and H zone shorten, but the A band length does not change.

options.text: A band shortens, I band remains constant
options.explanation: The A band does not shorten; it is the length of the thick filaments.

options.text: Both I band and A band shorten
options.explanation: Only the I band and H zone shorten.
The H zone narrows or disappears.

explanation.overview: According to the sliding filament theory, during contraction, thin filaments slide past thick filaments, shortening the sarcomere. The I band and H zone shorten, while the A band stays the same.
explanation.highYield: Contraction: I band ↓, H zone ↓, A band unchanged; sarcomere shortens.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Excessive sarcomere shortening can lead to muscle injury.

questions.question: Which protein anchors thin filaments to the Z disc?

options.explanation: α‑actinin cross‑links actin filaments at the Z disc.
Titin anchors thick filaments to the Z disc.
Dystrophin links the cytoskeleton to the sarcolemma.
Myomesin is at the M line.

explanation.overview: α-actinin is a major protein of the Z disc that cross-links the plus ends of actin filaments from adjacent sarcomeres, maintaining the structural integrity of the sarcomere.
explanation.highYield: α-actinin = Z disc protein; anchors actin.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mutations in α-actinin can cause cardiomyopathies.

questions.question: Titin is a giant elastic protein that spans from the Z disc to the M line and functions to:

options.text: Provide elasticity and stabilize thick filaments
options.explanation: Titin acts as a molecular spring and centers myosin during contraction.
Calcium release is regulated by the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

explanation.overview: Titin (connectin) is the largest known protein, extending from the Z disc to the M line. It acts as a molecular spring, maintaining the central position of the A band and providing passive elasticity.
explanation.highYield: Titin = giant elastic protein; Z disc to M line; passive tension.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Titin mutations cause titinopathies, a form of muscular dystrophy.

questions.question: In skeletal muscle, the triad consists of:

options.text: One T‑tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum
options.explanation: The triad is essential for excitation‑contraction coupling.
That would be a diad, found in cardiac muscle.
Triad refers to membrane structures, not myofibrils.
Not the definition of a triad.

explanation.overview: In skeletal muscle, the triad is formed by one T-tubule (invagination of sarcolemma) lying between two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, located at the A-I junction.
explanation.highYield: Triad = 1 T-tubule + 2 terminal cisternae; skeletal muscle; A-I junction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Disruption of triads impairs excitation-contraction coupling.

questions.question: Cardiac muscle differs from skeletal muscle by the presence of:

options.explanation: Cardiac muscle has T‑tubules associated with a single cisterna (diad) rather than two.
Cardiac cells usually have one or two central nuclei.
Cardiac muscle has SR, though less developed.

explanation.overview: Cardiac muscle has T-tubules located at Z-lines, forming diads (one T-tubule + one SR cisterna), whereas skeletal muscle has triads at A-I junctions.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac: diad at Z-line; Skeletal: triad at A-I junction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Cardiac diad dysfunction contributes to heart failure.

questions.question: The sarcoplasmic reticulum stores:

options.explanation: The SR sequesters and releases Ca²⁺ to regulate contraction.
Sodium ions are more important for the action potential.
Glycogen is stored in the cytoplasm.

explanation.overview: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialized smooth endoplasmic reticulum in muscle that actively pumps Ca²⁺ into its lumen (via SERCA pumps) and releases it (via ryanodine receptors) to trigger contraction.
explanation.highYield: SR = Ca²⁺ storage and release; regulates contraction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Malignant hyperthermia results from defective SR calcium release.

questions.question: Which of the following muscles is under voluntary control?

options.explanation: Skeletal muscle is voluntary; cardiac and smooth are involuntary.

explanation.overview: Skeletal muscle is innervated by the somatic nervous system and is under conscious (voluntary) control. Cardiac and smooth muscles are controlled by the autonomic nervous system and are involuntary.
explanation.highYield: Skeletal = voluntary; Cardiac and smooth = involuntary.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Loss of voluntary muscle control occurs in motor neuron diseases.

questions.question: Smooth muscle contraction is triggered by a rise in cytosolic Ca²⁺, which binds to:

options.explanation: Ca²⁺ binds calmodulin, which activates myosin light chain kinase to phosphorylate myosin.
Troponin C is the calcium sensor in striated muscle.
MLCK is the enzyme activated by Ca²⁺-calmodulin.

explanation.overview: Unlike striated muscle, smooth muscle lacks troponin. Ca²⁺ binds to calmodulin, forming a complex that activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), which phosphorylates myosin light chains, enabling actin-myosin interaction.
explanation.highYield: Smooth muscle: Ca²⁺ → calmodulin → MLCK → myosin phosphorylation → contraction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Smooth muscle relaxants (e.g., nitrates) work by reducing intracellular calcium or inhibiting MLCK.

questions.question: In skeletal muscle, Ca²⁺ binds to which protein to initiate contraction?

options.explanation: Troponin C binds Ca²⁺, causing a conformational change that moves tropomyosin away from actin‑binding sites.
Tropomyosin blocks binding sites, not binding Ca²⁺.
Calmodulin is the Ca²⁺ sensor in smooth muscle.
Myosin does not directly bind Ca²⁺.
Actin provides the binding site for myosin.

explanation.overview: In striated muscle, the troponin complex on the thin filament regulates contraction. Troponin C binds Ca²⁺, causing tropomyosin to shift, exposing the myosin-binding sites on actin.
explanation.highYield: Skeletal/cardiac: Ca²⁺ → troponin C → tropomyosin moves → contraction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Troponin I and T are released into blood after myocardial infarction, used as diagnostic markers.

questions.question: The dense bodies in smooth muscle are analogous to:

options.explanation: Dense bodies anchor actin filaments and are functionally similar to Z‑lines.

explanation.overview: Dense bodies are intracellular and membrane-associated structures in smooth muscle that serve as attachment points for thin filaments and intermediate filaments, functionally analogous to Z discs.
explanation.highYield: Dense bodies = Z disc equivalent in smooth muscle; anchor actin.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Dense body proteins are targets for research into smooth muscle disorders.

questions.question: Which connective tissue layer surrounds an individual skeletal muscle fiber?

options.explanation: Endomysium is a thin layer of reticular fibers surrounding each muscle cell.
Fascia is a general term for connective tissue sheets.
Sarcolemma is the cell membrane of the muscle fiber.

explanation.overview: Skeletal muscle has three connective tissue layers: endomysium (around individual fibers), perimysium (around fascicles), and epimysium (around the whole muscle).
explanation.highYield: Endomysium = single fiber; Perimysium = fascicle; Epimysium = whole muscle.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Inflammation of these layers (myositis) can be seen in autoimmune diseases.

questions.question: The perimysium surrounds:

explanation.overview: The perimysium is a thicker connective tissue layer that divides the muscle into fascicles (bundles of fibers) and contains larger blood vessels and nerves.
explanation.highYield: Perimysium = around fascicles; contains vessels and nerves.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Perimysial inflammation is characteristic of certain inflammatory myopathies.

questions.question: Cardiac muscle fibers are typically:

options.text: Branched with one or two central nuclei
options.explanation: Cardiac myocytes are branched and usually uninucleate (sometimes binucleate) with central nuclei.

explanation.overview: Cardiac muscle cells are branched, striated, and typically have one (occasionally two) centrally located nucleus. They are connected by intercalated discs.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac: branched, 1-2 central nuclei, intercalated discs.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Cardiac myocyte hypertrophy leads to enlarged nuclei (boxcar nuclei).

questions.question: Gap junctions in cardiac muscle are primarily located in:

options.text: Intercalated discs (fascia adherens and maculae adherens)
options.explanation: Gap junctions within intercalated discs allow electrical coupling.
They are part of the intercalated disc, which is a specialization of the sarcolemma.

explanation.overview: Intercalated discs have transverse portions (fascia adherens and desmosomes) and lateral portions rich in gap junctions, which allow the rapid spread of action potentials between cardiac cells.
explanation.highYield: Gap junctions in intercalated discs = electrical coupling; functional syncytium.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Gap junction remodeling contributes to arrhythmias.

questions.question: The M line of the sarcomere contains which protein that cross‑links thick filaments?

options.explanation: Myomesin connects myosin filaments at the M line.
Titin runs through the M line but myomesin is the cross-linking protein.
Nebulin is associated with thin filaments.
α-actinin is at the Z disc.

explanation.overview: The M line is a dense line in the center of the sarcomere where myomesin and other proteins (M-protein, obscurin) cross-link the thick filaments, maintaining their alignment.
explanation.highYield: M line = myomesin; cross-links thick filaments.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: M line proteins are relatively stable; their disruption is less common but can affect sarcomere stability.

questions.question: In which muscle type are T‑tubules located at the A‑I junction?

options.explanation: In skeletal muscle, T‑tubules are at the A‑I junction; in cardiac, they are at Z‑lines.
Skeletal muscle has them at A-I junction.

explanation.overview: In mammalian skeletal muscle, T-tubules are located at the A-I junction, and there are two per sarcomere. In cardiac muscle, T-tubules are at the Z-line, and there is one per sarcomere.
explanation.highYield: Skeletal: T-tubule at A-I junction (2/sarcomere); Cardiac: at Z-line (1/sarcomere).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: This difference is important in understanding excitation-contraction coupling.

questions.question: Smooth muscle cells contain intermediate filaments composed of:

options.explanation: Desmin is the main intermediate filament in smooth muscle, connecting dense bodies.
Lamin is in the nuclear lamina.
Actin is a microfilament, not an intermediate filament.

explanation.overview: The intermediate filaments in smooth muscle are mainly desmin (also vimentin in some types). They connect dense bodies and plaques, forming a cytoskeletal network that transmits force.
explanation.highYield: Smooth muscle IF = desmin; links dense bodies.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Desmin mutations can cause myopathies affecting smooth and skeletal muscle.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of cardiac muscle?

options.explanation: Cardiac myocytes typically have one central nucleus; peripheral nuclei are typical of skeletal muscle.
Cardiac muscle has many mitochondria for aerobic metabolism.

explanation.overview: Cardiac muscle has one or two central nuclei, is striated, rich in mitochondria, has intercalated discs, and can contract spontaneously (automaticity). Multinucleated peripheral nuclei are features of skeletal muscle.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac: 1-2 central nuclei, striated, intercalated discs, automaticity.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Loss of automaticity or abnormal automaticity leads to arrhythmias.

questions.question: The sarcolemma of a muscle fiber invaginates to form:

options.explanation: T‑tubules are deep invaginations that conduct action potentials into the fiber.
SR is a separate organelle, not an invagination.
Terminal cisternae are part of the SR.
Caveolae are small invaginations in smooth muscle.

explanation.overview: T-tubules are finger-like invaginations of the sarcolemma that penetrate deep into the muscle fiber, allowing the action potential to reach the terminal cisternae of the SR rapidly.
explanation.highYield: T-tubules = sarcolemma invaginations; carry action potential into fiber.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: T-tubule dysfunction is seen in some forms of heart failure.

questions.question: Rigor mortis occurs due to:

options.text: Lack of ATP preventing detachment of cross‑bridges
options.explanation: Without ATP, myosin heads remain bound to actin, causing stiffness after death.
Calcium release initiates contraction, but ATP depletion maintains it.
Acetylcholine initiates contraction at the NMJ, but rigor is due to ATP depletion.
Actin breakdown would not cause contraction.
SR rupture releases calcium, but rigor results from ATP depletion.

explanation.overview: After death, ATP production ceases. Without ATP, myosin heads cannot detach from actin, resulting in persistent cross-bridge binding and muscle stiffness, known as rigor mortis.
explanation.highYield: Rigor mortis = no ATP → myosin can't detach → persistent contraction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Rigor mortis timing is used in forensic medicine to estimate time of death.

questions.question: Fast‑twitch (type II) skeletal muscle fibers are characterized by:

options.text: Low myoglobin content, few mitochondria, glycolytic metabolism
options.explanation: Type II fibers are white, fast, and glycolytic; type I are red, slow, and oxidative.

options.text: High myoglobin, many mitochondria, oxidative metabolism

options.explanation: Type I fibers have more lipid.

explanation.overview: Type II (fast-twitch) fibers rely on anaerobic glycolysis, have fewer mitochondria and less myoglobin (white fibers), and are used for short bursts of power. Type I (slow-twitch) fibers are aerobic, red, and fatigue-resistant.
explanation.highYield: Type II: white, glycolytic, fast, fatigable; Type I: red, oxidative, slow, fatigue-resistant.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Muscle fiber type composition influences athletic performance and susceptibility to atrophy.

questions.question: Dystrophin is a protein that links:

options.text: The actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix via dystroglycan
options.explanation: Dystrophin connects the subsarcolemmal actin to the dystroglycan complex, stabilizing the membrane.
Desmin and other proteins link Z discs.

explanation.overview: Dystrophin is a large subsarcolemmal protein that connects the actin cytoskeleton to the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (DGC), which links to the extracellular matrix. This stabilizes the sarcolemma during contraction.
explanation.highYield: Dystrophin = actin → DGC → ECM; stabilizes sarcolemma.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by a lack of dystrophin, leading to muscle degeneration.

questions.question: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by mutations in the gene for:

options.explanation: Lack of functional dystrophin leads to muscle fiber damage and degeneration.
Dystroglycan mutations cause congenital muscular dystrophies.

explanation.overview: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the DMD gene that encodes dystrophin. Without dystrophin, the sarcolemma is fragile, leading to muscle necrosis.
explanation.highYield: DMD = dystrophin deficiency; X-linked; progressive muscle weakness.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Creatine kinase levels are markedly elevated in DMD due to muscle damage.

questions.question: Which muscle type exhibits spontaneous rhythmic contractions and is under autonomic control?

options.explanation: Cardiac is one, but not the only one.
Smooth muscle is also capable of this.
Both cardiac and smooth muscle are involuntary and can exhibit autorhythmicity.
Cardiac and smooth muscle both show autorhythmicity.

explanation.overview: Cardiac muscle (pacemaker cells) and some smooth muscle (e.g., gastrointestinal tract) exhibit spontaneous rhythmic contractions (autorhythmicity) and are regulated by the autonomic nervous system.
explanation.highYield: Autorhythmicity: cardiac (SA node) and single-unit smooth muscle (gut).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Disorders of autorhythmicity cause cardiac arrhythmias and gastrointestinal dysmotility.

questions.question: In skeletal muscle, each myofibril is surrounded by:

options.explanation: The sarcoplasmic reticulum forms a sleeve around each myofibril.
Mitochondria are between myofibrils but not a sleeve.
T-tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma.
The sarcolemma surrounds the entire fiber.
Endomysium is external to the sarcolemma.

explanation.overview: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a mesh-like network of tubules that surrounds each myofibril, storing and releasing calcium for contraction.
explanation.highYield: SR sleeves each myofibril; terminal cisternae form triads.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: SR stress is involved in muscle fatigue and some myopathies.

questions.question: The functional unit of contraction in smooth muscle is not a sarcomere because:

options.text: Actin and myosin are arranged in a lattice without Z‑lines
options.explanation: Smooth muscle lacks sarcomeres; filaments attach to dense bodies and slide via a different mechanism.
They are organized but not into sarcomeres.
It is calcium-dependent but via calmodulin.

explanation.overview: Smooth muscle lacks the regular sarcomeric organization of striated muscle. Actin and myosin filaments form a lattice anchored to dense bodies and membrane plaques, sliding past each other via the phosphorylation of myosin.
explanation.highYield: Smooth muscle: no sarcomeres; dense bodies anchor filaments.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: This arrangement allows smooth muscle to contract over a greater length range than striated muscle.

questions.question: Which of the following stains is commonly used to demonstrate striations in skeletal muscle?

options.explanation: PTAH highlights cross‑striations and intercalated discs.
H&E shows striations but not as distinctly.
Silver stains reticular fibers and neurons.

explanation.overview: PTAH (phosphotungstic acid-hematoxylin) stains cross-striations of skeletal muscle deep blue and also highlights intercalated discs in cardiac muscle.
explanation.highYield: PTAH = muscle striations and intercalated discs.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: PTAH is used to identify cross-striations in rhabdomyosarcoma.

questions.question: In a transverse section of skeletal muscle, the 'Cohnheim's area' refers to:

options.explanation: Cohnheim's areas are the cut ends of myofibrils seen in cross‑section.

explanation.overview: Cohnheim's fields (or areas) are the polygonal groupings of myofibrils seen in cross-sections of skeletal muscle fibers, separated by sarcoplasm, giving a mosaic appearance.
explanation.highYield: Cohnheim's areas = cross-sectional myofibril bundles in skeletal muscle.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Loss of Cohnheim's areas occurs in severe muscle atrophy.

questions.question: The motor end plate is a specialized synapse between:

options.text: Motor neuron and skeletal muscle fiber
options.explanation: The neuromuscular junction transmits signals from nerve to skeletal muscle.

options.text: Smooth muscle cell and autonomic nerve
options.explanation: Smooth muscle has varicosities, not motor end plates.

explanation.overview: The neuromuscular junction (motor end plate) is the synapse between the terminal bouton of a motor neuron and the sarcolemma of a skeletal muscle fiber, where acetylcholine is released to initiate contraction.
explanation.highYield: Motor end plate = NMJ; acetylcholine release; junctional folds.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Myasthenia gravis is caused by autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the motor end plate.

questions.question: Acetylcholine receptors at the motor end plate are clustered on:

options.explanation: Receptors are concentrated at the tops of junctional folds.
Receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane.
Schwann cells cover the nerve terminal.
Synaptic vesicles are in the presynaptic terminal.

explanation.overview: The postsynaptic sarcolemma is thrown into deep junctional folds. Acetylcholine receptors are densely packed at the crests of these folds, while voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated in the troughs.
explanation.highYield: ACh receptors at crests of junctional folds; sodium channels in troughs.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies destroy these receptors, reducing neuromuscular transmission.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about smooth muscle gap junctions?

options.text: They allow electrical coupling and coordinated contraction
options.explanation: Partially true, but need the complete answer.

options.text: They are absent in multi‑unit smooth muscle
They are present in visceral (single‑unit) smooth muscle

options.explanation: Visceral smooth muscle (e.g., gut) has gap junctions; multi‑unit (e.g., iris) lacks them.

explanation.overview: Smooth muscle is classified into single-unit (visceral) and multi-unit types. Single-unit smooth muscle has abundant gap junctions, allowing coordinated contraction. Multi-unit smooth muscle has few or no gap junctions, with each cell innervated individually.
explanation.highYield: Single-unit smooth muscle: gap junctions present; Multi-unit: few/no gap junctions.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Gap junction blockers could theoretically affect smooth muscle contractility.

questions.question: The H zone of the sarcomere contains:

options.explanation: The H zone is the central region of the A band with only myosin.
That's the rest of the A band.
Z discs are at the ends.
The M line is in the center of the H zone, but the H zone is the entire region of only thick filaments.

explanation.overview: The H zone (Hensen's zone) is the lighter central part of the A band where only thick (myosin) filaments are present, without overlapping thin filaments. It shortens during contraction.
explanation.highYield: H zone = thick filaments only; in the center of A band; shortens during contraction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The H zone is visible in relaxed sarcomeres and disappears during maximal contraction.

questions.question: In cardiac muscle, the transverse tubules are larger and located at the:

options.explanation: Cardiac T‑tubules are at Z‑lines and often form diads with SR.

explanation.overview: Cardiac T-tubules are wider than those of skeletal muscle, located at the Z-line rather than the A-I junction. They typically associate with a single sarcoplasmic reticulum cisterna to form a diad.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac T-tubules: at Z-line, form diads (1 SR cisterna).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: T-tubule loss or remodeling occurs in heart failure.

questions.question: The term 'sarcoplasm' refers to the:

options.explanation: Sarcoplasm is the cytoplasm of muscle fibers.

options.text: Cell membrane of a muscle cell

options.explanation: Nuclei are organelles within the sarcoplasm.

explanation.overview: Sarcoplasm is the cytoplasm of muscle cells, containing myofibrils, mitochondria, glycogen, and myoglobin. The prefix 'sarco-' refers to muscle.
explanation.highYield: Sarcoplasm = muscle cytoplasm; sarcolemma = membrane; sarcoplasmic reticulum = ER.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Sarcoplasmic masses are sometimes seen in certain myopathies.

questions.question: Myoglobin is an oxygen‑binding protein found in:

options.explanation: Myoglobin stores and facilitates oxygen diffusion in muscle.
Hemoglobin is in red blood cells; myoglobin is in muscle.
Mitochondria use oxygen, but myoglobin is in the cytoplasm.

explanation.overview: Myoglobin is a cytoplasmic hemoprotein in muscle cells that binds oxygen, facilitating its diffusion and providing a short-term oxygen store. It gives red muscle its color.
explanation.highYield: Myoglobin = oxygen storage in muscle; abundant in type I fibers.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Elevated serum myoglobin after muscle injury can cause acute kidney injury (rhabdomyolysis).

questions.question: Which of the following muscles is an example of multi‑unit smooth muscle?

options.explanation: Multi‑unit smooth muscle (iris, vas deferens) has discrete units innervated individually.
Uterine smooth muscle behaves like single-unit.

explanation.overview: Multi-unit smooth muscle consists of individual motor units, each cell innervated separately, allowing fine control. Examples include the iris, ciliary muscle, vas deferens, and arrector pili muscles.
explanation.highYield: Multi-unit smooth muscle: iris, ciliary muscle, vas deferens; independent innervation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Autonomic drugs can target specific multi-unit smooth muscle (e.g., atropine dilating pupils).

questions.question: In skeletal muscle, the region of the sarcolemma that invaginates to form T‑tubules is the:

options.explanation: In mammals, T‑tubules are at the A‑I junction.
Z disc is where T-tubules are in cardiac muscle.
T-tubules are at the junction of A and I bands.

explanation.overview: In mammalian skeletal muscle, T-tubules are precisely located at the A-I junction, with two T-tubules per sarcomere. This ensures that depolarization reaches the terminal cisternae simultaneously.
explanation.highYield: Skeletal T-tubules at A-I junction (2/sarcomere).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Proper T-tubule positioning is essential for efficient excitation-contraction coupling.

questions.question: Caveolae are numerous in the sarcolemma of:

options.explanation: Caveolae may function like rudimentary T‑tubules in smooth muscle.

explanation.overview: Caveolae are flask-shaped membrane invaginations rich in cholesterol and caveolin. In smooth muscle, they are abundant and are thought to function as primitive T-tubules, involved in calcium signaling.
explanation.highYield: Caveolae in smooth muscle = T-tubule equivalent; calcium influx.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Caveolin mutations are associated with some smooth muscle disorders.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of slow oxidative (type I) muscle fibers?

options.text: High myoglobin content, rich in mitochondria, fatigue‑resistant
options.explanation: Type I fibers are red, oxidative, and used for posture.

explanation.overview: Type I (slow oxidative) fibers have high myoglobin (red), many mitochondria, and high oxidative enzyme capacity. They are slow-contracting, fatigue-resistant, and used for sustained activity like posture.
explanation.highYield: Type I: red, oxidative, slow, fatigue-resistant; Type II: white, glycolytic, fast, fatigable.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Disuse atrophy preferentially affects type II fibers.

questions.question: The dense bands to which thin filaments attach in smooth muscle are called:

options.explanation: Dense bodies are intracellular structures analogous to Z‑lines.
Z discs are in striated muscle.
Gap junctions are for cell communication.

explanation.overview: Smooth muscle contains cytoplasmic dense bodies (containing α-actinin) and membrane-associated dense plaques where thin filaments and intermediate filaments attach, serving as the functional equivalent of Z discs.
explanation.highYield: Dense bodies = Z disc analogs; anchor actin in smooth muscle.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Dense body proteins are potential targets for smooth muscle pharmacology.

questions.question: Which protein regulates contraction in smooth muscle by phosphorylation of myosin light chains?

options.explanation: MLCK phosphorylates myosin to permit cross‑bridge cycling.
Calmodulin binds Ca²⁺ but MLCK performs the phosphorylation.
Caldesmon is a regulatory protein but MLCK is the primary kinase.

explanation.overview: Smooth muscle contraction is triggered when Ca²⁺-calmodulin activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), which phosphorylates the regulatory light chains of myosin, enabling actin-myosin interaction.
explanation.highYield: Ca²⁺-CaM → MLCK → myosin phosphorylation → contraction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: MLCK inhibitors are being explored as smooth muscle relaxants.

questions.question: In cardiac muscle, the plateau phase of the action potential is due to:

options.text: Slow calcium influx through L‑type channels
options.explanation: Calcium entry prolongs depolarization, preventing tetanus.
The exchanger contributes but the plateau is primarily L-type calcium current.

explanation.overview: The cardiac action potential has a prolonged plateau phase (phase 2) caused by the balance between inward L-type calcium current and outward potassium current. This prolonged depolarization prevents tetanic contraction.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac plateau = L-type Ca²⁺ influx; prevents tetanus.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Calcium channel blockers (verapamil) affect the plateau phase, reducing contractility.

questions.question: The term 'sarcopenia' refers to:

options.text: Age‑related loss of skeletal muscle mass
options.explanation: Sarcopenia is the degenerative loss of muscle with aging.

explanation.overview: Sarcopenia is the progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength with aging, beginning around age 30-40 and accelerating after 60. It increases the risk of falls and frailty.
explanation.highYield: Sarcopenia = age-related muscle loss; treatable with exercise and nutrition.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Sarcopenia is a major contributor to disability in the elderly.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of the sarcomere?

options.explanation: Dystrophin is beneath the sarcolemma, not part of the sarcomere.
Nebulin is associated with thin filaments.

explanation.overview: The sarcomere is composed of thick filaments (myosin), thin filaments (actin), and associated structural proteins (titin, nebulin, myomesin, α-actinin). Dystrophin is a subsarcolemmal protein linking the cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix.
explanation.highYield: Sarcomere proteins: actin, myosin, titin, nebulin, α-actinin. Dystrophin is extrasarcomeric.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is due to dystrophin deficiency, not a sarcomeric protein defect directly.

questions.question: The region where actin and myosin filaments overlap is the:

options.explanation: Overlap occurs in the lateral parts of the A band.
M line is the center of the sarcomere.

explanation.overview: The A band is the full length of the thick filaments. The outer regions of the A band contain both thick and thin filaments overlapping, while the central H zone has only thick filaments.
explanation.highYield: Overlap = lateral A band; I band = actin only; H zone = myosin only.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The extent of overlap determines the force-length relationship.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the structure of a triad in skeletal muscle?

options.text: Central T‑tubule with two terminal cisternae
options.explanation: The triad is essential for rapid calcium release.

options.text: Central terminal cisterna with two T‑tubules
A single T‑tubule and one cisterna

explanation.overview: The skeletal muscle triad consists of a central T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum at the A-I junction, enabling rapid Ca²⁺ release upon depolarization.
explanation.highYield: Triad = 1 T-tubule + 2 terminal cisternae; A-I junction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Triad disruption in some congenital myopathies leads to weakness.

questions.question: In smooth muscle, contraction is initiated by Ca²⁺ binding to calmodulin, which then activates:

options.explanation: Ca²⁺‑calmodulin activates MLCK, which phosphorylates myosin.
Troponin C is in striated muscle.

explanation.overview: The Ca²⁺-calmodulin complex binds to and activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), which phosphorylates the regulatory light chain of myosin II, enabling its interaction with actin and initiating contraction.
explanation.highYield: Ca²⁺ → CaM → MLCK → myosin-P → contraction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: MLCK is a target for smooth muscle relaxation (e.g., nitric oxide pathway).

questions.question: Which of the following is characteristic of cardiac muscle but not skeletal muscle?

options.explanation: Intercalated discs are unique to cardiac muscle.
Skeletal has multiple peripheral nuclei; cardiac has 1-2 central nuclei.

explanation.overview: Intercalated discs are complex cell junctions unique to cardiac muscle, containing fascia adherens, desmosomes, and gap junctions. They are not present in skeletal or smooth muscle.
explanation.highYield: Intercalated discs = cardiac only.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Disruption of intercalated discs occurs in myocardial infarction.

questions.question: The function of nebulin in skeletal muscle is to:

options.text: Act as a molecular ruler for thin filaments
options.explanation: Nebulin determines the length of actin filaments.

explanation.overview: Nebulin is a giant protein that spans the length of the thin filament, acting as a molecular ruler that determines the precise length of actin filaments in skeletal muscle sarcomeres.
explanation.highYield: Nebulin = molecular ruler for thin filament length.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Nebulin mutations cause nemaline myopathy.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the M line?

options.text: It contains myomesin and cross‑links thick filaments
options.explanation: The M line stabilizes the array of thick filaments.

options.text: It is the site of actin filament anchoring

options.explanation: The M line does not shorten.

options.text: It is absent in cardiac muscle
options.explanation: Cardiac muscle also has M lines.

explanation.overview: The M line is in the center of the sarcomere, composed of myomesin and other proteins that cross-link the thick filaments, maintaining their hexagonal arrangement.
explanation.highYield: M line = myomesin; cross-links thick filaments; center of sarcomere.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: M line integrity is important for force transmission.

questions.question: The sarcolemma of a muscle fiber is surrounded by:

options.explanation: The basal lamina lies just outside the sarcolemma, and the endomysium surrounds it.

explanation.overview: Each skeletal muscle fiber is surrounded by a basal lamina (external lamina) and then by the endomysium, a delicate layer of reticular connective tissue. The basal lamina contains components for repair and regeneration.
explanation.highYield: Sarcolemma surrounded by basal lamina + endomysium.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Satellite cells reside between the sarcolemma and basal lamina and are crucial for muscle regeneration.

questions.question: In a routine H&E section, smooth muscle appears as:

options.text: Spindle‑shaped cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and central nuclei
options.explanation: Smooth muscle cells are fusiform with central nuclei and lack striations.

options.text: Long cylindrical cells with peripheral nuclei

explanation.overview: Smooth muscle in H&E appears as bundles of spindle-shaped cells with abundant eosinophilic (pink) cytoplasm and a single, elongated, central nucleus. No cross-striations are visible.
explanation.highYield: Smooth muscle: spindle cells, central nuclei, eosinophilic, no striations.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Leiomyomas are benign tumors of smooth muscle, easily identified by these features.

questions.question: The dense plaques on the cytoplasmic side of smooth muscle sarcolemma are analogous to:

options.explanation: Dense plaques anchor actin filaments to the membrane, similar to hemidesmosomes.
Desmosomes anchor intermediate filaments between cells.
Adherens junctions anchor actin between cells, not to the matrix.

explanation.overview: Smooth muscle dense plaques are submembranous structures that anchor actin filaments and intermediate filaments to the sarcolemma. They are functionally similar to hemidesmosomes, which anchor epithelial cells to the basement membrane.
explanation.highYield: Dense plaques = hemidesmosome analogs; anchor filaments to membrane.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Dense plaque proteins may be altered in some smooth muscle pathologies.

questions.question: In which condition would you expect to see increased numbers of central nuclei in skeletal muscle fibers?

options.explanation: Regenerating fibers show central nuclei (like myotubes).
Atrophy does not typically cause central nuclei.
Denervation causes grouped atrophy, not central nuclei.

explanation.overview: Central nuclei are a hallmark of regenerating muscle fibers (myotubes) and are also seen in certain myopathies (centronuclear myopathy). Normal mature fibers have peripheral nuclei.
explanation.highYield: Central nuclei = regeneration or centronuclear myopathy.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Biopsy showing central nuclei suggests muscle regeneration or a congenital myopathy.

questions.question: The pacemaker of the heart is the sinoatrial node, which is composed of:

options.text: Modified cardiac muscle cells with fewer myofibrils
options.explanation: SA node cells are small, pale-staining, with fewer contractile elements but high automaticity.
Purkinje fibers are part of the conduction system, not the primary pacemaker.

explanation.overview: The sinoatrial (SA) node consists of specialized, small, modified cardiac muscle cells that spontaneously depolarize, setting the heart rate. They have fewer myofibrils and a slower action potential upstroke.
explanation.highYield: SA node = primary pacemaker; modified cardiac cells with automaticity.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Sick sinus syndrome results from SA node dysfunction.

questions.question: Purkinje fibers are specialized cardiac muscle cells located in the:

options.explanation: Purkinje fibers are large, pale-staining cells under the endocardium.
They are distributed throughout ventricular subendocardium.

explanation.overview: Purkinje fibers are large, glycogen-rich cardiac muscle cells located in the subendocardial layer of the ventricles. They conduct impulses rapidly to coordinate ventricular contraction.
explanation.highYield: Purkinje fibers: subendocardial, large, pale, few myofibrils, rapid conduction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Purkinje fibers are part of the ventricular conduction system; damage can cause conduction defects.

questions.question: Skeletal muscle fibers that attach to bones via tendons are termed:

options.explanation: Extrafusal fibers are the main force-generating fibers.
Intrafusal fibers are in muscle spindles.

explanation.overview: Extrafusal muscle fibers are the standard force-producing skeletal muscle fibers innervated by alpha motor neurons and attached to bones via tendons. Intrafusal fibers are found within muscle spindles.
explanation.highYield: Extrafusal fibers = main muscle fibers; α-motor neuron innervation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Intrafusal fibers are sensory, part of the stretch reflex.

questions.question: The A band appears dark under the light microscope because:

options.text: It contains thick filaments which are anisotropic (birefringent)
options.explanation: A band = anisotropic band; appears dark in polarized light and dense in H&E.
I band has only thin filaments.

options.text: It is the region of overlap only
options.explanation: Overlap is part of the A band.

explanation.overview: The A band contains the entire length of the thick myosin filaments, which are anisotropic (birefringent) under polarized light, hence the name 'A' band. In H&E, it stains more darkly due to protein density.
explanation.highYield: A band = anisotropic; thick filaments; dark in H&E.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: A band visibility is used to assess sarcomeric integrity in electron micrographs.

questions.question: Satellite cells in skeletal muscle are:

options.text: Stem cells located between the sarcolemma and basal lamina
options.explanation: Satellite cells are quiescent myogenic stem cells responsible for muscle repair and regeneration.

explanation.overview: Satellite cells are small, mononuclear cells located between the sarcolemma and basal lamina of skeletal muscle fibers. They are stem cells that proliferate and fuse to form new muscle fibers after injury.
explanation.highYield: Satellite cells = muscle stem cells; under basal lamina; regeneration.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Satellite cell exhaustion contributes to sarcopenia and poor muscle healing in muscular dystrophy.

questions.question: In smooth muscle, the latch state refers to:

options.text: Prolonged maintenance of force with low ATP consumption
options.explanation: Smooth muscle can maintain tone for long periods with minimal energy use.
Smooth muscle does not exhibit tetanus.

explanation.overview: The latch state is a unique property of smooth muscle where cross-bridges remain attached for extended periods with reduced ATP consumption, allowing sustained tone (e.g., in blood vessels) without fatigue.
explanation.highYield: Latch state = sustained force with low ATP; unique to smooth muscle.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The latch state is important for maintaining vascular tone and blood pressure.

questions.question: Cardiac muscle contains an abundance of which organelle for its high energy demands?

options.explanation: Cardiac muscle is highly aerobic and rich in mitochondria.

explanation.overview: Cardiac myocytes contain numerous mitochondria, occupying up to 40% of the cell volume, reflecting their almost exclusively aerobic metabolism and continuous contractile activity.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac muscle: rich in mitochondria; aerobic metabolism.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in heart failure and cardiomyopathies.

questions.question: Which protein in smooth muscle inhibits myosin ATPase activity in the absence of calcium?

options.explanation: Caldesmon binds actin-tropomyosin and inhibits myosin ATPase in resting smooth muscle.
Myomesin is in the M line.

explanation.overview: Caldesmon is a thin filament-associated protein in smooth muscle that, together with tropomyosin, inhibits actin-myosin interaction in the absence of Ca²⁺/calmodulin. Phosphorylation of caldesmon relieves this inhibition.
explanation.highYield: Caldesmon = smooth muscle inhibitory protein; binds actin-tropomyosin.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Caldesmon is used as an immunohistochemical marker for smooth muscle differentiation.

questions.question: In skeletal muscle, the energy for cross-bridge cycling is provided by:

options.explanation: Myosin heads have ATPase activity that provides energy for the power stroke.
Calcium triggers contraction but doesn't provide energy.
Not a direct energy source for contraction.

explanation.overview: Myosin heads bind ATP and hydrolyze it to ADP and inorganic phosphate, providing the energy for the conformational change (power stroke) that moves actin filaments.
explanation.highYield: ATP → myosin ATPase → cross-bridge cycling.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Rigor mortis occurs when ATP is depleted.

questions.question: The term 'myotendinous junction' refers to the site where:

options.text: Muscle fibers connect to tendons via extensive interdigitations
options.explanation: The myotendinous junction is a specialized interface that transmits force from muscle to tendon.

explanation.overview: At the myotendinous junction, the sarcolemma of the muscle fiber is thrown into numerous folds, and collagen fibers of the tendon insert into these folds, providing a strong, force-transmitting connection.
explanation.highYield: Myotendinous junction = muscle-tendon interface; high stress point.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Strains often occur at or near the myotendinous junction.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the histological appearance of skeletal muscle in cross-section?

options.text: Polygonal fibers with peripheral nuclei and punctate myofibrils
options.explanation: In cross-section, fibers are polygonal, with peripheral nuclei and Cohnheim's areas representing myofibrils.

options.text: Rounded cells with central nuclei in palisades

explanation.overview: Transverse sections of skeletal muscle show large polygonal fibers with multiple peripheral nuclei. The cytoplasm contains numerous punctate dots (Cohnheim's areas) representing myofibrils in cross-section.
explanation.highYield: Cross-section: polygonal fibers, peripheral nuclei, Cohnheim's areas.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Muscle biopsy in cross-section is used to assess fiber size, type, and pathology.

questions.question: What is the role of calsequestrin in skeletal muscle?

options.text: Calcium-binding protein in the terminal cisternae of SR
options.explanation: Calsequestrin buffers calcium inside the SR, allowing high-capacity storage.
Ryanodine receptor is the release channel.

explanation.overview: Calsequestrin is a high-capacity, low-affinity calcium-binding protein in the lumen of the sarcoplasmic reticulum terminal cisternae. It sequesters large amounts of Ca²⁺, reducing the free Ca²⁺ gradient against which the SERCA pump must work.
explanation.highYield: Calsequestrin = SR Ca²⁺ buffer; in terminal cisternae.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mutations in calsequestrin are linked to certain forms of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT).

questions.question: During muscle development, myoblasts fuse to form multinucleated myotubes. Which regulatory proteins drive this process?

options.text: Myogenic regulatory factors (MyoD, myogenin, Myf5, MRF4)
options.explanation: These transcription factors orchestrate skeletal muscle differentiation.

explanation.overview: Skeletal muscle development (myogenesis) is regulated by basic helix-loop-helix transcription factors known as myogenic regulatory factors: MyoD, Myf5, myogenin, and MRF4, which induce muscle-specific gene expression.
explanation.highYield: Myogenesis: MyoD, Myf5 (determination); myogenin, MRF4 (differentiation).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Rhabdomyosarcoma expresses myogenic regulatory factors, used in diagnosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about red and white muscle fibers?

options.text: Red fibers have more myoglobin and mitochondria; white fibers have more glycogen
options.explanation: Red fibers (type I) are oxidative; white fibers (type II) are glycolytic.

options.text: White fibers are slower than red fibers
White fibers have more blood capillaries
Red fibers have less myoglobin than white fibers

explanation.overview: Red (type I, slow oxidative) fibers are rich in myoglobin and mitochondria, using oxidative phosphorylation, and are fatigue-resistant. White (type II, fast glycolytic) fibers rely on glycolysis, have less myoglobin, and are fatigable.
explanation.highYield: Red = type I, oxidative, myoglobin-rich, fatigue-resistant. White = type II, glycolytic, fast, fatigable.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Fiber type conversion can occur with training or disease.

questions.question: Smooth muscle contraction can be regulated by which of the following mechanisms?

options.text: Autonomic nerves, hormones, stretch, and local factors
options.explanation: Smooth muscle is regulated by multiple inputs, including neural, hormonal, and mechanical stimuli.
Multiple neurotransmitters and hormones regulate it.
Calcium is the mediator, but regulation is broader.

explanation.overview: Smooth muscle tone and contraction are controlled by autonomic nerves (sympathetic and parasympathetic), circulating hormones (epinephrine, angiotensin), local metabolites (NO, prostaglandins), and mechanical stretch (myogenic response).
explanation.highYield: Smooth muscle regulation: neural, hormonal, mechanical, local factors.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Antihypertensives often target smooth muscle regulation (e.g., calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors).

questions.question: The connective tissue layer that surrounds an entire muscle is the:

options.explanation: Epimysium is the dense irregular connective tissue sheath around the whole muscle.
Fascia is a more general term for connective tissue sheets.

explanation.overview: The epimysium is the dense irregular connective tissue that wraps the entire muscle, continuous with the tendon. It contains the larger blood vessels and nerves supplying the muscle.
explanation.highYield: Epimysium = whole muscle sheath; continuous with tendon.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The epimysium is involved in compartment syndrome.

questions.question: In electron microscopy, the triad junction is characterized by:

options.text: Periodic electron-dense structures (feet) between T-tubule and SR membranes
options.explanation: These feet are the ryanodine receptors (calcium release channels) on the SR.
The membranes are closely apposed but not fused.
Gap junctions are between cells, not at the triad.

explanation.overview: The triad junction shows T-tubule membrane closely apposed to terminal cisterna membrane, with electron-dense 'foot' structures spanning the gap. These feet are the cytoplasmic domains of ryanodine receptors (RyR1) on the SR and dihydropyridine receptors (DHPR) on the T-tubule.
explanation.highYield: Triad feet = RyR1 (SR) and DHPR (T-tubule); excitation-contraction coupling.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Malignant hyperthermia is caused by RyR1 mutations.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about cardiac muscle contraction is true?

options.text: Cardiac muscle cannot undergo tetanus due to its long refractory period
options.explanation: The prolonged plateau phase prevents summation and tetanic contraction.

options.text: Cardiac muscle contracts only when stimulated by nerves
Cardiac muscle relies on anaerobic glycolysis primarily
Cardiac muscle has peripheral nuclei like skeletal muscle

explanation.overview: The long refractory period (due to the plateau phase of the action potential) of cardiac muscle prevents summation and tetanus, ensuring rhythmic pumping without sustained contraction.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac muscle: long refractory period → no tetanus; essential for heart function.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Arrhythmias disrupt normal refractory periods.

questions.question: In smooth muscle, the enzyme that dephosphorylates myosin light chain, promoting relaxation, is:

options.explanation: MLCP removes the phosphate, deactivating myosin and allowing relaxation.
PKA can phosphorylate MLCK, but not the direct phosphatase.
Troponin I is in striated muscle.

explanation.overview: Relaxation of smooth muscle occurs when myosin light chain phosphatase (MLCP) dephosphorylates the myosin regulatory light chains, reducing actin-myosin interaction. This is a key regulatory step.
explanation.highYield: MLCP → dephosphorylate myosin → relaxation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Rho-kinase inhibits MLCP, promoting contraction; Rho-kinase inhibitors are being explored for vasodilation.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about skeletal muscle motor units?

options.text: A single motor neuron innervates multiple muscle fibers
options.explanation: A motor unit consists of one motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates.

options.text: Each muscle fiber is innervated by multiple motor neurons
options.explanation: Each fiber is innervated by only one motor neuron.

options.text: Motor units are only found in cardiac muscle
options.explanation: Cardiac muscle has gap junctions, not motor units.

options.text: A motor unit always contains only one fiber

options.explanation: Motor units are motor, not sensory.

explanation.overview: A motor unit is the functional unit of skeletal muscle, consisting of a single alpha motor neuron and all the skeletal muscle fibers it innervates. Small motor units allow fine control; large motor units provide force.
explanation.highYield: Motor unit = 1 motor neuron + its muscle fibers.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Motor unit recruitment is the basis for increasing muscle force.

questions.question: The cell membrane of a cardiac muscle cell is called the:

options.explanation: Like skeletal muscle, the cardiac muscle cell membrane is the sarcolemma.

options.text: Plasmalemma (generic term, but sarcolemma is specific)
options.explanation: While plasmalemma is the general term, muscle cells specifically use sarcolemma.
Neurolemma is the Schwann cell sheath.

explanation.overview: Both skeletal and cardiac muscle cells have a specialized plasma membrane called the sarcolemma. Smooth muscle cells also use this term.
explanation.highYield: Sarcolemma = plasma membrane of muscle cells.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Dystrophin links the cytoskeleton to the sarcolemma.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about smooth muscle compared to skeletal muscle?

options.text: Smooth muscle can contract to a smaller fraction of its resting length
options.explanation: Smooth muscle can shorten to a much greater extent than skeletal muscle.

options.text: Smooth muscle uses troponin for regulation

explanation.overview: Smooth muscle has a much wider length-tension relationship than skeletal muscle, allowing it to generate force over a greater range of lengths. This is crucial for hollow organ function (e.g., bladder filling).
explanation.highYield: Smooth muscle: greater shortening capacity; no sarcomeres.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: This property allows organs like the bladder to accommodate large volume changes while maintaining tone.

questions.question: The sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump (SERCA) functions to:

options.text: Transport Ca²⁺ from the cytosol back into the SR lumen
options.explanation: SERCA actively pumps calcium into the SR, reducing cytosolic calcium and causing relaxation.

options.text: Export calcium out of the cell
options.explanation: That's the sarcolemmal Ca²⁺-ATPase or Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger.

explanation.overview: SERCA (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase) is an ATP-dependent pump that transports Ca²⁺ from the cytosol into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, lowering cytosolic calcium and promoting muscle relaxation.
explanation.highYield: SERCA = calcium reuptake into SR; relaxation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: SERCA activity is reduced in heart failure, contributing to diastolic dysfunction.

questions.question: Muscle spindles are encapsulated sensory receptors that detect:

options.explanation: Muscle spindles are proprioceptors sensing muscle length and rate of change.

explanation.overview: Muscle spindles are encapsulated structures containing modified muscle fibers (intrafusal fibers) innervated by sensory and motor nerves. They detect the stretch and length of the muscle, essential for proprioception and the stretch reflex.
explanation.highYield: Muscle spindle = stretch receptor; intrafusal fibers; proprioception.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The knee-jerk reflex tests muscle spindle function.

questions.question: Skeletal muscle contraction is initiated by the release of which neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction?

options.explanation: ACh binds to nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate, depolarizing the sarcolemma.
Norepinephrine is for smooth and cardiac muscle.

explanation.overview: At the neuromuscular junction, the motor neuron releases acetylcholine (ACh), which binds to nicotinic ACh receptors on the sarcolemma, causing sodium influx and depolarization, leading to an action potential and contraction.
explanation.highYield: ACh → nicotinic receptors → depolarization → contraction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Myasthenia gravis involves autoantibodies against ACh receptors.

questions.question: In cardiac muscle, the atrioventricular (AV) node is located in the:

options.text: Interatrial septum near the tricuspid valve
options.explanation: The AV node is in the floor of the right atrium, near the coronary sinus.
That's where the bundle of His runs.
AV node is a discrete structure.

explanation.overview: The AV node is a compact mass of specialized cardiac muscle cells in the posteroinferior region of the interatrial septum, near the opening of the coronary sinus. It slows impulse conduction to allow ventricular filling.
explanation.highYield: AV node: right atrium, near tricuspid valve; delays impulse.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: AV nodal block results in varying degrees of heart block.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about cardiac muscle metabolism?

options.text: It relies primarily on fatty acid oxidation under resting conditions
options.explanation: Cardiac muscle uses fatty acids as its main fuel source, with some glucose and lactate.
Fatty acids are a major fuel.
Lactate production is minimal at rest.

explanation.overview: Cardiac muscle is a metabolic omnivore but preferentially uses fatty acids (60-70% of ATP) under resting conditions. It also uses glucose, lactate, and ketone bodies. It is obligatorily aerobic.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac fuel: mainly fatty acids, then glucose; obligate aerobic.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In heart failure, metabolism shifts toward glucose utilization.

questions.question: Myoepithelial cells are contractile cells found in:

options.explanation: Myoepithelial cells surround secretory acini and ducts, helping expel secretions.

explanation.overview: Myoepithelial cells are star-shaped, contractile cells of epithelial origin located between the basal lamina and secretory cells in glands (salivary, sweat, mammary, lacrimal). They contract to help expel secretions.
explanation.highYield: Myoepithelial cells = contractile, aid secretion; salivary, sweat, mammary.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Myoepithelial cells are used to distinguish in situ from invasive breast carcinoma.

questions.question: The sliding filament theory explains muscle contraction as:

options.text: Thin and thick filaments sliding past each other without changing their length
options.explanation: Actin filaments slide over myosin filaments, shortening the sarcomere.

options.text: Muscle fibers folding like an accordion
Myosin filaments detaching from the Z disc

explanation.overview: The sliding filament theory (Huxley, 1954) states that during contraction, actin (thin) filaments slide past myosin (thick) filaments, increasing overlap and shortening the sarcomere, while the filaments themselves remain the same length.
explanation.highYield: Sliding filament: actin slides over myosin; sarcomere shortens; filaments constant length.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: This is the fundamental mechanism of all muscle contraction.

questions.question: Which of the following muscle types exhibits the greatest capacity for regeneration?

options.explanation: Smooth muscle retains the ability to divide and regenerate throughout life.
Skeletal muscle can regenerate via satellite cells, but smooth muscle has greater regenerative capacity.
Cardiac muscle has very limited regenerative capacity.

explanation.overview: Smooth muscle cells retain the ability to divide throughout life (hyperplasia). Skeletal muscle can regenerate via satellite cells but has limits. Cardiac muscle has negligible regenerative capacity, healing by scar formation.
explanation.highYield: Regeneration: smooth > skeletal > cardiac (minimal).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Myocardial infarction causes permanent scar; skeletal muscle injuries can heal if the basal lamina is intact.
